commons:441106.summary: Beneath the Latin text of the psalm, Christ, with a cross-nimbus and a red cloak, stands in the dress of a soldier holding a book and a cross-staff whose point he drives down on the beasts at his feet: a serpent-like dragon and a lion. An angel at the left raises its hands in wonder and a hand reaches from the heavens at the upper right. The miniature reads the psalm as a prophecy of Christ's victory over evil.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter (Cod. Bibl. fol. 23) was made around 820 at Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris and contains 316 illustrations of the Psalms; the 'fol23' in the file name is the manuscript's shelfmark, not the folio.
This miniature illustrates Psalm 91 (90):13 on folio 107v: 'super aspidem et basiliscum ambulabis et conculcabis leonem et draconem'.
The verse was sung daily at Compline and in the Roman Good Friday liturgy, which helped make the image of Christ trampling the beasts a symbol of his triumph over Satan.

met:468482.summary: This marble head of a mature man with a full, curling beard and long hair falling to the shoulders was carved in the Roman manner and, according to the Metropolitan Museum, later transformed; it may represent Zeus, or Christ, or a Zeus image reworked as Christ. It vividly illustrates how the bearded, majestic image of Christ drew on the long tradition of classical images of the father of the gods.
facts: The Met dates the head to the 3rd or 4th century with a later transformation, and titles it 'Head of Christ or Zeus', leaving the identification open.
The bearded, long-haired type of Christ that became standard from the late 4th century onward owes much to classical images of Zeus and of philosophers.
met:468482.notes: Identification as Christ is uncertain (the museum itself hedges). Kept because the Met lists 'Christ' as a subject, but an editor may prefer to exclude it.
